name: Endolymphatic Pressure Cascade Rifle
description:
The EPCR-3 operates by projecting a tightly collimated beam of modulated infrasonic pressure waves tuned precisely to the resonant frequency of the endolymphatic fluid within the inner ear. Upon exposure, the fluid undergoes rapid oscillatory pressure cycling, overwhelming the vestibular system and triggering catastrophic spatial disorientation, nausea, and full postural collapse within seconds. The effect is entirely invisible — no projectile, no flash, no audible report above a low subsonic thrum.

What distinguishes the EPCR-3 from cruder acoustic suppression tools is its adaptive targeting firmware, which samples ambient environmental acoustics and dynamically adjusts the emission envelope to compensate for hard surfaces, wind shear, and intervening crowd noise. At ranges under forty meters, it achieves near-total vestibular disruption even through standard hearing protection. At longer ranges, the effect degrades to sustained nausea and impaired balance — still tactically significant.

Zheng-Dao Bioelectric engineered the weapon initially as a crowd suppression platform for high-value transit corridor security, but the design escaped controlled licensing within eighteen months of its first deployment. Street copies exist, though they lack the adaptive firmware and frequently cause permanent vestibular damage at close range — an outcome the original design actively attempts to avoid, if only for liability purposes.
specifications:
effective range: 8–42 meters
power source: High-density capacitor cell, 28 discharge cycles per charge
emission frequency: 0.4–18 Hz, dynamically modulated
onset time: 1.8–4 seconds at full exposure
weight: 3.1 kg
form factor: Bullpup carbine, matte polymer housing
acoustic signature: Sub-threshold for standard hearing; felt as pressure at close range
tactical_use: Operators use the EPCR-3 as a breach-clearing tool, disabling room occupants before entry without triggering audible alarms or leaving ballistic evidence. It is particularly favored in situations where incapacitation without lethality is legally or contractually required. Security teams use it to collapse fleeing targets in open corridors. Paired with a suppressed sidearm, it constitutes a near-silent takedown platform. Operators are trained to fire in short bursts and reposition, as sustained emission in enclosed spaces can cause reflected pressure buildup affecting the operator.
cultural_context: Among GLMZ's corporate security culture, the EPCR-3 occupies a strange moral position — marketed as humane, frequently used brutally. Carrying one signals institutional backing; the weapon is too expensive and too legally encumbered for most freelancers to acquire legitimately. On the street, knockoff versions are called 'spinners' and are associated with a particularly cruel class of debt enforcer who prefers to leave targets helpless rather than dead. Medical examiners have begun flagging suspicious inner ear scarring in assault victims as a distinct forensic signature.
known_users: Underground pit-fight fixers who use it to neutralize opponents pre-match
story_hooks: A series of seemingly random collapses in a crowded market district turns out to be an operator testing range on civilians before a high-profile contract hit.
A knockoff EPCR-3 is sold to a freelancer with a factory defect that locks it at maximum intensity — the seller has already disappeared.
A corporate whistleblower claims Zheng-Dao's 'humane' firmware intentionally logs target biometric data during each discharge and sells it to third parties.
An investigator begins connecting multiple assault victims by their identical vestibular scarring — someone is using the same weapon across very different criminal contexts.

physical_description.visual_profile: A compact bullpup carbine with an organic, almost skeletal aesthetic. The frame curves and tapers unnaturally, suggesting biomechanical engineering rather than conventional firearms design. The emission aperture dominates the forward profile—a wide, flared muzzle that looks more like a speaker horn than a barrel. No visible bolt, charging handle, or traditional mechanical complexity; instead, the body is dominated by smooth, flowing polymer surfaces interrupted only by discrete sensor arrays and a minimal control interface.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length: 58 cm; barrel/emission chamber: 22 cm; width at widest (grip): 8 cm; height with mounted display: 16 cm
physical_description.weight_description: Deceptively light in hand—3.1 kg distributed along the bullpup frame creates perfect balance. Feels like it's made of air despite its solid construction. Users describe it as 'impossibly easy to shoulder,' with no muzzle heaviness whatsoever.
physical_description.primary_material: Advanced polymer composite (ZHENG-DAO proprietary thermoplastic reinforced with carbon-fiber threads), aluminum alloy subframe for sensor mounts and internal waveguide structure
physical_description.finish: Matte tactical black polymer with subtle anthracite weathering in high-contact areas. The aluminum internal structures visible through cutout windows show brushed gunmetal patina. No reflective surfaces—engineered for minimal visual signature.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary: deep charcoal matte black; Secondary: brushed aluminum gray (visible in sensor mounting rings and waveguide elements); Accent: faint teal LED glow from the adaptive targeting array (visible only when powered)
physical_description.grip_texture: Rubberized polymer with fine crosshatch texture for secure purchase even in wet environments. The grip is substantially curved, almost organic, with a palm swell that feels almost biological.
distinctive_features: Wide, flared emission aperture (22 cm diameter) resembling a speaker horn—no traditional barrel
Recessed sensor array along the top rail with pinhole microphones and pressure-calibration points
Small liquid-crystal display inset into the charging area showing frequency readout and power state
Three discrete venting slots along the left side (thermal dissipation for capacitor banks)
Absence of a visible trigger guard—trigger is a pressure-sensitive pad recessed into the grip
Waveguide cutout windows showing internal aluminum resonance chambers (aesthetic + functional weight reduction)
Faint thermal bloom patterns etched into polymer near the aperture from factory thermal cycling tests
ZHENG-DAO nameplate in minimal sans-serif font on the right side of the receiver, barely raised above the surface
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: ZHENG-DAO BIOELECTRIC stamped in minimal gray lettering on the right side of the polymer housing, approximately 12 cm from the aperture. Serial number and compliance codes laser-etched into an inconspicuous aluminum plate recessed into the grip. Manufacturing date encoded as a QR microprint near the capacitor access panel (visible only under magnification).
physical_description.condition_typical: Operators maintain the EPCR-3 in meticulous condition—any polymer scoring or aperture degradation directly affects targeting precision. Well-used examples show fingerprint oils on the grip and minor thermal stress marks around the sensor array. Battle-worn units are rare; the weapon is too specialized and too restricted for sustained field wear. When damaged, it is typically retired rather than field-repaired.
